name: Ergonomic setup (monitor at eye level)
lead: An ergonomic desk setup with the monitor at eye level is a posture practice in which people raise the screen so the head stays upright rather than tilting down. In posture and looksmaxxing communities it is described as a way to avoid so-called tech neck, a forward-head position associated with the neck and jawline.

Ergonomics is the scientific discipline that studies interactions between people and the systems they work in, aiming to improve well-being and performance; the term was used by Wojciech Jastrzębowski in 1857 and revived in English in 1949 [1][2].
The sources reviewed contain general ergonomics material and no trial of monitor height specifically, nor any examining appearance outcomes.

paras: Ergonomic guidance generally emphasizes neutral body postures, avoiding awkward static positions, and fitting the work setup to the person [1]. Monitor-at-eye-level is a commonly repeated workstation tip; the sources reviewed do not give specific monitor-height guidance. Wikipedia notes that adjustable furniture such as sit-stand desks, along with training, breaks and assessments, are typical workplace measures [2].

Tools such as the Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA), published in 1993, score neck, trunk and upper limb postures to flag work-related upper limb disorder risk [3]. A meta-analysis of surgeons and interventionalists found high prevalence of work-related musculoskeletal disorders in that group, reflecting sustained neck-flexed postures [4]. Evidence on workstation changes is mixed: Wikipedia reports that several studies of new workstations found improved well-being while many others found no marked health improvement [2].
No studies found testing monitor height for appearance outcomes. General ergonomics research on musculoskeletal symptoms exists, as described above [2][3][4].

timeline.event: Wojciech Jastrzębowski publishes the term ergonomics [1][2].
Term adopted in English at a UK Admiralty meeting [2].

quick.overview:
This practice means raising your monitor so your head stays upright instead of tilting down. People discuss it as a way to avoid tech neck.

Ergonomics research focuses on workplace musculoskeletal symptoms. Evidence on workstation changes is mixed and nothing reviewed tests appearance.
quick.mechanism: The idea is that a neutral head position reduces sustained neck flexion and strain, and posture tools like RULA score neck angle as a risk factor.
quick.risks: No notable risks are described. Practice here is a low-cost workstation adjustment.
